subject: Pathology Markers
title: Renal Function: Serum Creatinine, eGFR & BUN/Cr Ratio
preview: Renal function tests require trend, baseline kidney disease and hemodynamic context; no single urine index proves the cause of AKI.

sections.title: Know the limitations of creatinine and urea
points: Serum creatinine reflects production and renal handling; muscle mass and illness can alter its interpretation.
Urea is influenced by protein turnover, volume depletion and gastrointestinal bleeding and should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic discriminator.

sections.title: Structured AKI assessment
points: Compare serial kidney function, fluid balance and urine output; review medications and exposure to contrast or toxins.
Assess volume status, examine urine sediment when indicated and use ultrasound if obstruction is suspected.

sections.title: Exam trap: FENa is not a verdict
points: Urine sodium and fractional excretion may be altered by diuretics or mixed renal pathology.
A low FENa does not invariably exclude intrinsic renal disease, and a high FENa does not always exclude a prerenal component.

quickRevision: Acute kidney injury may develop before creatinine rises noticeably; urine output and changes from baseline also matter.
Fractional excretion indices can support the assessment of sodium handling but may be misleading with diuretics, chronic kidney disease and sepsis.
Evaluate perfusion, nephrotoxins, obstruction and urine sediment alongside laboratory results.

quiz.question: Why can serum creatinine lag behind acute changes in renal function?
options: It changes instantaneously with every nephron injury
It accumulates over time after a fall in GFR
It is independent of muscle mass
quiz.explanation: It accumulates over time after a fall in GFR. Serum creatinine reflects production and renal handling; muscle mass and illness can alter its interpretation.
